Statement of compliance
For the purposes of this report, Hollard Holdings Australia Pty Ltd (Hollard, Hollard 
Group, HHA, we, us or our) represents both the Australian and New Zealand 
businesses, and HNZ represents the New Zealand branch only, which is in scope for 
this reporting.
This Climate-related Disclosure Statement (this Statement) is made by The Hollard 
Insurance Company Pty Ltd (a subsidiary of HHA) New Zealand Branch (NZBN 942 
904 212 9851, NZ Company No. 5869665) (HNZ), pursuant to the Financial Markets 
Conduct Act 2013 (the Act) for the financial year 1 July 2023 to 30 June 2024 
(Reporting Period). This statement complies with Aotearoa New Zealand Climate 
Standards (NZ CS 1, 2 and 3) issued by the External Reporting Board (XRB). 
For our inaugural report, we have sought independent technical guidance from 
an external climate advisory team in the preparation of this climate disclosure 
statement. 
Notwithstanding this year is our first year of climate reporting, we have made 
tangible headway towards the development of a sustainability strategy (known 
as the “Shared Value Strategy & Roadmap”, see details in Strategy section of the 
statement), that will allow Hollard to position itself successfully as the global and 
domestic economy transitions towards a low-emissions, climate-resilient future 
state.

5
Adoption provisions
There are first-time adoption provisions in the Aotearoa New Zealand Climate 
Standards 2 (Adoption of Aotearoa New Zealand Climate Standards; ‘NZ CS 2’). In 
preparing our first-year climate-related disclosure for HNZ, we have invoked the 
following Adoption Provisions 1-7 in NZ CS 2 as tabled below:
The adoption of these provisions in the first year allows us additional time to further 
develop these requirements of the climate statements for HNZ reporting for the 
year ended 30 June 2025 (FY25). We have used this first year to better understand 
our climate-related risks and opportunities and will continue our work towards 
quantifying our current and anticipated financial impacts, metrics and targets over 
time. 
Approved and signed on behalf of The Hollard Insurance Company Pty Ltd Board on 
23 September 2024.

Disclaimer
This report contains forward looking 
statements including climate scenario 
analyses, estimations and forecasts of physical 
and transition risks across multiple time 
horizons based on climate hazard projections 
for HNZ as of 30 June 2024.  In using climate 
projections provided by our external climate 
advisory team, HNZ acknowledges that they are 
based on assumptions about future greenhouse 
gas emissions associated with human activity 
and other policy choices. 
The climate projections do not attempt to 
predict the timing of meteorological events 
such as storms, droughts, or floods. Projections 
vary from model to model in producing the 
climate scenario analysis, therefore the 
external climate advisory team referenced 
a range of projections from multiple models: 
Intergovernmental Panel for Climate Change 
(IPCC) - Representative Concentration 
Pathways, NASA-NEX, World Meteorological 
Organisation, New Zealand’s National Institute 
for Weather and Atmospheric Research (NIWA) 
and Climate Change Commission. 
Introduction
HNZ operates as a New Zealand branch of 
the Australian company The Hollard Insurance 
Company Pty Ltd (ABN 78 090 584 473) (HIC), a 
licensed insurer under the Insurance (Prudential 
Supervision) Act 2010.  Hollard Holdings 
Australia Pty Ltd. (ABN 30 154 586 802) (HHA, 
Hollard or Hollard Group) is HIC’s immediate 
parent company. 
HNZ operates an “agency” model, where third 
party agency partners are delegated authority 
to undertake various activities on behalf of 
Hollard, such as servicing customers and 
intermediaries, claims management, pricing and 
underwriting. HNZ underwrites a broad range 
of general insurance products, including motor, 
home, contents, business, bicycle and pet 
insurance.

Governance
The Hollard Group’s Board has oversight of climate-related risks and opportunities within Hollard 
in accordance with our governance framework. This flows from monitoring of the Group’s revised 
sustainability strategy (known as the “Shared Value Strategy & Roadmap”) which considers 
climate-related strategy.
The Hollard Group’s Board has delegated certain responsibilities in relation to climate risk oversight 
to Board Committees as set out in the Hollard Climate Governance Oversight and Responsibilities 
diagram below. This year, Hollard has uplifted its approach to oversight of climate risk, updating the 
charters of the Board and Board Committees with their respective responsibilities.  See Figure 1. 
Climate Governance Oversight and Responsibilities, and Figure 2. HNZ’s Climate Risk Management 
for details. 
The Board’s revised sustainability strategy includes progressing our business towards its climate 
resilience goals in the future. In FY24, the Board Audit Committee (BAC) has received updates 
through standing quarterly meetings, in relation to climate-related impacts, climate scenario 
analysis across time horizons and other climate-related disclosure milestones. Qualitative 
Environment, Social and Governance (ESG) KPIs for assessing the performance of the Executive 
Leadership Team (ELT) were included in FY24. The Board Remuneration Committee (RemCo) 
discussed and recommended for approval to the Board FY25 KPIs, which will align to the revised 
sustainability strategy.

Strategy.

Strategy
HNZ shares an overarching strategy with the 
broader Hollard Group. The Hollard Group is 
driving a significant strategic transformation 
journey, consolidating core systems to 
drive both efficiencies and better customer 
outcomes through process simplification and 
product innovation. Hollard’s focus over the 
next few years will shift from implementing 
these technologies towards leveraging the 
scale and efficiency opportunities they provide 
and building impactful insurance innovation 
for our customers, partners, and communities. 
Externally, the impact of increasing frequency 
of natural perils, continued claims inflation 
and heightened regulatory focus will remain 
challenging for Hollard and the wider insurance 
industry. Hollard will need to continue 
considering climate-related risks as part of its 
insurance risk management practices across 
product, pricing, underwriting, reinsurance, and 
claims. 
Shared Value is a way to think about how we do 
well by doing good, how we become a catalyst 
for enduring, positive, social change while 
running a sustainable and profitable business 
by looking at how we make decisions and how 
we think about our role not just in the economy 
but the wider global community. Hollard’s 
Shared Value Strategy & Roadmap enables us 
to identify and understand sustainability risks 
and opportunities (including climate change). 
In FY24, Hollard refreshed 
the articulation of its 
corporate strategy 
to drive alignment in 
investment and effort 
across its focus areas. 
One of the key strategic 
principles underpinning 
the strategy is the Shared 
Value principle. 
Below are the embedded climate-related goals:
•	 Ensure the effects of climate change are 
routinely considered in all of our business, 
investment and underwriting decisions 
•	 Incentivise and reward customers who take 
steps to mitigate the effects of climate 
change 
Hollard has also intentionally aligned its 
sustainability initiatives with the Insurance 
Council of New Zealand (ICNZ) and the 
Insurance Council of Australia (ICA), ensuring 
we contribute to industry collaboration 
on climate change issues in a consistent 
approach.
Climate scenario analysis
In FY24, Hollard established the Climate-related 
Disclosure Working Group (CRD WG) to support 
mandatory climate-related disclosures in New 
Zealand and Australia. The CRD WG consisted 
of senior management from Commercial, 
Operations, Legal and Governance, Risk and 
Compliance, Actuarial and Group Analytics 
and Finance Functions chaired by the Head of 
Accounting, Reporting and Tax. The CRD WG 
was governed by the CRD Steering Committee 
(SteerCo) made up of the Group Chief Risk 
Officer (CRO), Chief Commercial Officer (CCO), 
Chief Financial Officer (CFO) and Chief Executive 
Officer’s (CEO) Executive Advisor ensuring 
appropriate oversight of the program delivery, 
decisioning and compliance to the Aotearoa 
New Zealand Climate Standards. This included 
the presentation and endorsement of the 
climate scenario analysis to the Board Audit 
Committee and Board in March 2024.
The external climate advisory team facilitated 
more than 10 Climate Workshops with the CRD 
WG to test our exposure and vulnerability to 
climate-related physical and transition risks by 
adopting three climate scenarios (see top row 
headings in Table 2. scenario analysis) from 
internationally recognised sources, such as the 
IPCC and the Network for Greening the Financial 
System (NGFS).

HNZ selected 2030, 2040, 2050 as the time 
horizons for climate scenario analysis, based 
on the tenure of HNZ’s existing partnerships, 
and its strategic planning timeframe. The time 
horizons are 20-year averages around the 
nominated year, that is, 2030 is the average of 
2020 to 2039, 2050 is the average of 2040 to 
2059. 
While this is a standalone climate scenario 
analysis and has not been formally integrated 
within the Group’s strategy in FY24, impact 
of catastrophe risk on capital is assessed 
as part of Group’s regular scenario analysis 
and stress testing in line with Internal Capital 
Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP). The 
Group’s strategic planning is also performed on 
an ongoing basis, which seeks to examine our 
strengths, weaknesses, resource availabilities, 
opportunities against anticipatory risks and 
trends. 
When determining the global warming 
scenarios, HNZ considered:
•	 Industry specificity: ensuring our climate 
scenario analysis is aligned to the industry 
bodies, and to be easily compared with 
peers, as per XRB guidance. This led to 
the adoption of the Orderly (NGFS Net-Zero 
2050), Disorderly (NGFS Delayed Transition) 
and Hot House World (NGFS Current Policies) 
scenarios. 
•	 The requirements of NZ CS 1: NZ CS 1 
requires climate reporting entity to adopt 
a minimum of three warming scenarios, 
namely: “at a minimum, a 1.5 degrees Celsius 
climate-related scenario, a three degrees 
Celsius or greater climate-related scenario, 
and a third climate-related scenario”. 
•	 Inclusion of a balanced spread of the 
scenarios: low (average 1.5 degrees Celsius, 
[SSP1- RCP 1.9]), medium (average 2.7 
degrees Celsius, [SSP2 – RCP 4.5]), and 
high warming (average 3.6 degrees Celsius, 
[SSP3 – RCP 7.0]) scenarios.
Climate-related physical and  
transition impacts
Physical climate-related risks
Physical climate-related risks describe the 
effect of increasing in frequency and severity 
of physical hazards such as extreme rain and 
floods, cyclones and storms, storm surges, 
bushfires, and sea level rise. The impact can 
subsequently cause an increase in claims, 
reinsurance costs and net loss ratios.
HNZ has no property, plant and equipment or 
right-of-use lease assets, therefore no physical 
assets are exposed to climate-related risks. 
However, HNZ is exposed to climate hazards 
through the impact of our insured assets 
(motor and homes) across the value chain. 
Hollard has undertaken an assessment of the 
following physical hazards on the New Zealand 
business and operations:
•	 Acute physical hazards: extreme rain and 
flood, bushfires, storms, and cyclones
•	 Chronic physical hazards: rising sea-level, 
and increasing in temperature 
The key finding of 
Hollard’s climate risk 
assessment is that 
extreme weather 
events may lead to 
an increase cost of 
claims, increased 
insurance product 
pricing, and related 
non-renewals, resulting 
in market contractions 
and revenue loss. 
13

14
The increasing frequency and intensity of 
weather events over time may outstrip Hollard’s 
ability to provide the expected levels of service, 
while also impacting on the availability of 
service providers. Both impacts have potential 
to undermine Hollard’s reputation and could 
potentially result in portfolio attrition due to 
customer defection, and a loss of market share.
Transition climate-related impacts
Hollard has also undertaken an assessment 
of transition risks across New Zealand and 
Australia. Transition Risks are identified in line 
with the four categories outlined in Task Force 
on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD)
guidance, assessing the risk of transitioning 
to a lower-carbon economy to address climate 
mitigation and adaptation:
•	 Policy and Legal 
•	 Technology
•	 Market
•	 Reputation
The highest-rated Market risk is associated 
with Hollard’s risk of keeping up with changing 
consumer preferences for insurance products 
that either incentivise decarbonisation or 
support resilience building. Over time market 
share loss may result as consumers switch to 
other insurers offering more climate-responsive 
products.
In FY24, HNZ has not identified any climate-
related opportunities that will materialise in 
the short term. However, we do anticipate there 
may be opportunities for us to innovate and 
offer products that are responsive to changing 
market and consumer sentiment; however, this 
would be a long-term opportunity for us. 
Transition plan
In FY24, HNZ has taken Adoption Provision 
3 to delay disclosing our Transition Plan. As 
part of embedding our sustainability strategy 
throughout FY25 and beyond, Hollard will look 
to better understand our carbon footprint, and 
position ourselves in line with the industry to 
decarbonise and respond to climate-related 
risks across the value chain to help transition 
towards a low-emission economy.

Risk
Management.

Risk Management  
Risk Management Framework
The Hollard Group maintains a Risk 
Management Framework (RMF) that provides 
a structure for identifying, assessing, and 
managing material risks to ensure Hollard is 
being prudently and appropriately managed 
having regard to the size, business mix and 
complexity of its operations. The Hollard 
Group’s RMF applies to all entities within Hollard 
(including HNZ) and considers risk management 
within its value chains. 
The Hollard Group Risk Management Strategy 
(RMS) and Risk Appetite Statement (RAS) are 
key components of the RMF. The RMS describes 
each material risk (both financial and non-
financial) and outlines Hollard’s approach to 
managing these risks. The RAS sets out the 
degree of risk Hollard is prepared to accept in 
pursuit of its strategic objectives and business 
plans and sets out an appetite for each of the 
material risks referenced in the RMS.    
The Hollard Group does not manage climate 
risk as a standalone material risk category 
but considers it in the assessment of 
the established RMS risk categories (e.g. 
Underwriting, Pricing, Catastrophe, Claims, 
Capital and Strategic Risks). Hollard focuses 
on the shorter time horizon (less than 1 year) in 
managing its material risks and will consider 
a longer-term horizon (more than 1 year) in 
managing its emerging material risks. 
The Hollard Group has not yet published 
explicit guidance or a policy on climate risk 
but is cognisant of regulatory guidance, and 
recognises that a more integrated approach 
to climate risk management, including the 
compounding effect of physical, transition 
and liability risk in the long term is an area 
of opportunity that will be considered in the 
future.
Climate-related risk management 
processes, tools and methods
The Hollard Group’s approach to managing its 
material risks (including the consideration of 
the impact of climate-related risk) involves 
the assessment of each material risk, and 
its associated appetite against impact (both 
financial and non- financial), the likelihood of 
that risk occurring, and the estimated time that 
the impact of a risk may arise.
Hollard relies on a number of tools and methods 
to identify and to assess the scope and impact 
of climate-related risk on Hollard’s established 
risk categories. These include but are not 
limited to:  
•	 Natural peril pricing review: Hollard 
conducts an annual natural peril review 
across portfolios to ensure exposure for 
each peril is within tolerable range and to 
identify any new areas of risk;
•	 Capital modelling and management: impact 
of catastrophe risk (physical climate risk) 
on capital is considered and assessed as 
part of Hollard’s regular and ad-hoc stress 
testing in line with Hollard’s ICAAP. The 
stress scenarios considered included single 
extreme event as well as multiple large 
events;
•	 Catastrophe modelling: uses detailed risk 
and exposure information to model Hollard’s 
catastrophe risk exposure annually to inform 
pricing, reinsurance purchasing, capital 
modelling and budgeting;
•	 Embargo management: limits risk 
concentration where there is a high 
probability of a natural peril event;
•	 Quarterly aggregate exposure and peril 
monitoring: monitors Hollard’s (including 
HNZ) aggregate exposure to prevent 
unplanned growth in high event risk areas;
•	 Partner monitoring: provides partner 
oversight on risks, such as underwriting and 
pricing risk.

17
Climate risk management governance
The Hollard Group Board is ultimately responsible for Hollard’s RMF and oversees its operation by 
management. In particular, the Hollard Group Board is responsible for setting Hollard’s Risk Appetite 
and approving its RMS. 
HNZ related risk matters are incorporated within the Group’s Commercial function’s risk profile 
and are reviewed in the Commercial function’s risk forums quarterly. Material risks that require 
prioritised focus are reported to the quarterly HNZ Management Committee (HNZMC) and Hollard 
Group Financial Risk Committee (FRC). Material risks that require further escalation are then 
reported by the CRO to the BRC, or via the CEO HNZ Report to the Board. See Figure 2. for further 
details.

Metrics & Targets
GHG emissions
For the year ended 30 June 2024, HNZ has 
no Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions, and 
applied Adoption Provision 4 from NZ CS 2 to 
delay Scope 3 emissions disclosure.  HNZ also 
has no GHG emissions targets, industry-based, 
and intensity metrics to report. Our base year 
will commence in FY25 as scope 3 emission 
calculation takes place, which will assist us in 
setting more meaningful metrics to measure 
success. 
Measurement approach
HNZ has adopted the operational control 
consolidation approach under The Greenhouse 
Gas Protocol (GHG Protocol) in assessing our 
GHG emissions:
HNZ has no material owned or controlled 
physical assets in New Zealand, and our leased 
office falls outside of our operational control.  
No part of HNZ’s value chain has been excluded 
for assessing Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions.  
While having applied NZ CS 2 Adoption 
Provision 4 on all 15 categories of scope 3 
emissions (purchased goods and services, 
capital goods, fuel and energy-related 
activities, upstream transportation and 
distribution, waste generated in operations, 
business travel, employee commuting,

Measuring risks and opportunities
HNZ considers physical and transition risks to 
be material for its New Zealand insurance and 
reinsurance business operations in the short, 
medium and long term.  A qualitative analysis 
has been included in our Strategy section 
and we are working towards measuring our 
exposure to physical and transition risks and 
opportunities quantitatively in the near future.
HNZ currently has no New Zealand assets, 
investment, capital expenditure, or funding 
allocated directly towards climate-related 
risks and opportunities, and there have been 
no business activities or investment decisions 
aligned to climate-related opportunities. We 
plan to update our investment and capital 
strategy in line with our sustainability strategy, 
and drive the development of key metrics and 
targets in the next financial year.
Development of metrics and targets
As at the reporting period, we have not 
established any quantitative metrics or 
targets that measure climate-related risks 
and opportunities, and therefore monitoring, 
assessing and managing of them are not 
currently linked to management remuneration. 
Hollard’s RemCo will further align FY25 KPIs to 
the revised sustainability strategy, assessing 
how we perform against the strategic principles 
outlined in the Strategy section.

Appendix A:
Definitions.
(supplemented by NZ CS 3 Appendix A)
20

21
Climate-related risks: 
The potential negative impacts of climate change on an entity. 
ESG: 
Environment, Social and Governance
GHG: 
Greenhouse gas; The greenhouse gases listed in the Kyoto Protocol: carbon dioxide (CO2); methane (CH4), 
nitrous oxide (N2O), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), nitrogen trifluoride (NF3), perfluorocarbons (PFCs), and 
sulphur hexafluoride (SF6).
Material: 
Information is material if omitting, misstating or obscuring it could reasonably be expected to influence 
decisions that primary users make on the basis of an entity’s climate-related disclosures.
Physical risks: 
Risks related to the physical impacts of climate change. Physical risks emanating from climate change 
can be event-driven (acute) such as increased severity of extreme weather events. They can also relate to 
longer-term shifts (chronic) in precipitation and temperature and increased variability in weather patterns, 
such as sea level rise.
Scenario analysis: 
A process for systematically exploring the effects of a range of plausible future events under conditions of 
uncertainty. Engaging in this process helps an entity to identify its climate-related risks and opportunities 
and develop a better understanding of the resilience of its business model and strategy.
Target: 
A specific level, threshold, or quantity of a metric that an entity wishes to meet over a defined time horizon 
in order to achieve an entity’s overall climate-related ambition and strategy.
Transition plan: 
An aspect of an entity’s overall strategy that describes an entity’s targets, including any interim targets, and 
actions for its transition towards a low-emissions, climate resilient future.
Transition risks: 
Risks related to the transition to a low-emissions, climate-resilient global and domestic economy, such as 
policy, legal, technology, market and reputation changes associated with the mitigation and adaptation 
requirements relating to climate change.
Value chain: 
The full range of activities, resources and relationships related to an entity’s business model and the 
external environment in which it operates. A value chain encompasses the activities, resources and 
relationships an entity uses and relies on to create its products or services from conception to delivery, 
consumption and end of life. Relevant activities, resources and relationships include those in an entity’s 
operations, such as human resource; those along its supply, marketing and distribution channels, such as 
materials and service sourcing and product and service sale and delivery; and the financing, geographical, 
geopolitical and regulatory environments in which an entity operates.
